items.title: Trump warns 'whole civilization will die tonight' as Iran deadline nears

featured_image.name: Trump threatens to strike Iran's infrastructure if Strait of ...

items.description:
President Trump escalated his rhetoric against Iran on Tuesday, warning that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again" if Tehran does not agree to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by his 8 p.m. Eastern deadline. The ultimatum comes on the 38th day of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, which began on February 28 with what the White House called "Operation Epic Fury".[1][2][3][4][5]

Airstrikes hit two bridges and a train station inside Iran on Tuesday morning, while Iranian officials called on young people to form human chains around power plants Trump has threatened to destroy. Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, posted on X that 14 million Iranians had volunteered to fight and said he would join them.[2][6]

items.title: Wall Street firm sends analyst into Strait of Hormuz by speedboat

featured_image.name: The 'gimbal' gambit: An undercover analyst exposes the real truth ...

items.description:
Citrini Research, the small Wall Street firm that rattled markets earlier this year with a bearish call on artificial intelligence, has turned its unconventional methods toward the ongoing crisis in the Strait of Hormuz — dispatching a field analyst into one of the world's most dangerous waterways by speedboat to gather firsthand intelligence on Iranian shipping controls.

The firm said it sent an employee referred to as "Analyst #3" to Oman's Musandam Peninsula, where he boarded a GPS-less speedboat and pushed toward the center of the strait armed with $15,000 in cash and concealed recording equipment, according to The Wall Street Journal. The analyst traveled within view of the Iranian coastline, observing drones overhead and Iranian patrol boats operating nearby, before being intercepted and briefly detained. His phone was confiscated, and his observations were later reconstructed during an eight-hour debrief after he returned safely.[1][2]

items.description: Somalia is preparing to launch its first-ever offshore oil drilling operation, with a Turkish state-owned drillship expected to arrive in Somali waters later this week. The Çağrı Bey, operated by the Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO), is scheduled to reach Somalia around April 10, marking a milestone in a partnership that could reshape the economic prospects of one of the world's poorest nations.[1][2][3]

items.description: President Donald Trump has warned of the "total destruction" of Iran's bridges and power plants if Tehran does not reopen the Strait of Hormuz by midnight GMT on Tuesday, setting the stage for what could become a dramatic escalation in the five-week-old conflict. items.title: IEA chief says Middle East war will accelerate renewables shift

featured_image.name: International Energy Agency head says global economy faces 'major ...

items.description:
The worst energy crisis in modern history will ultimately speed the world's pivot to renewable energy, nuclear power, and electric vehicles, International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol predicted in an interview published Tuesday with the French newspaper Le Figaro.[1][2]

Birol described the current energy shock, triggered by the Middle East war and Iran's de facto blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, as "more serious than those of 1973, 1979 and 2022 combined". Yet the IEA executive director said there were "reasons to be optimistic" about how the upheaval would reshape the global energy system.[2][1]

items.title: Dangote refinery ramps up African exports amid Iran war

featured_image.name: Dangote to export maiden petrol cargo out of Africa ...

items.description:
Nigeria's Dangote refinery, the largest in Africa, has stepped up exports of gasoline and urea fertilizer to countries across the continent as supply disruptions caused by the war on Iran continue to squeeze global energy and commodity markets, owner Aliko Dangote said on Monday.[1][2]

The refinery, operating at its full capacity of 650,000 barrels per day, has shipped approximately 17 cargoes of gasoline to other African nations, with urea fertilizer exports also climbing as buyers scramble for alternatives to traditional Middle East and Gulf suppliers, according to Reuters. Dangote said the facility had helped cushion the crisis both in Nigeria and across the continent.[1]

items.title: Iran war energy shock accelerates global return to nuclear power

featured_image.name: Japan to restart world's biggest nuclear plant - Le Monde

items.description: The war between Israel and Iran has upended global energy markets, cutting off roughly one-fifth of the world's liquefied natural gas supply and prompting a rapid reassessment of nuclear energy across Asia and beyond. Countries that had retreated from atomic power after the 2011 Fukushima disaster are now racing to restart reactors, extend plant lifespans, and build new capacity as LNG prices surge and supply reliability crumbles.

items.title: Saudi Arabia closes Bahrain causeway after Iranian missile strikes

featured_image.name: King Fahd Causeway | bridge, Bahrain-Saudi Arabia | Britannica

items.description: Saudi Arabia shut down the King Fahd Causeway, the sole road link connecting it to Bahrain, early on Tuesday as Iranian ballistic missiles targeted the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province, according to the Associated Press. The closure came hours before a deadline set by President Donald Trump for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or face strikes on its power plants and bridges.[1][2]

items.title: Oil rises, futures slip as Trump's Iran deadline looms
items.description: Global markets entered a period of heightened tension on Tuesday as President Donald Trump's deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — set for 8 p.m. Eastern Time — loomed over trading floors worldwide. Oil prices climbed while U.S. equity futures slipped, and cryptocurrency markets wavered as investors weighed the prospect of a last-minute diplomatic breakthrough against the threat of a devastating military escalation.

items.title: King Fahd Causeway reopens after Iranian missile strikes on Saudi Arabia

featured_image.name: Saudi Arabia shuts key King Fahd Causeway linking Bahrain ...

items.description:
The King Fahd Causeway, the sole road link between Saudi Arabia and the island kingdom of Bahrain, reopened on Tuesday after a brief closure prompted by Iranian ballistic missile strikes targeting Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. The King Fahd Causeway Authority announced on X that traffic on the bridge was "back to normal after a temporary suspension" that had been imposed as a precautionary measure.[1]

The reopening came hours after authorities halted all vehicle movement across the 25-kilometer bridge in the early hours of Tuesday, as Iran launched seven ballistic missiles toward Saudi Arabia's eastern region. Saudi Arabia's defense ministry said it intercepted and destroyed the missiles, though debris fell near energy facilities. A major fire erupted at the Al Jubail Industrial City, the Middle East's largest industrial hub and a center of petrochemical and oil refining operations, after what open-source intelligence accounts described as a ballistic missile and drone attack.[2][3][4][5][6]
